title: Monaco Water Week: Freediving and Sea Kayak to Menton
subRegion: Monaco and the Alpes-Maritimes coast, Cap d'Ail to Menton

bestPeriod.note: Water is warmest and most freedive-friendly from July to September; June has clearer visibility and fewer tourist boats over the Posidonia meadows.

summary: A Monaco-based week pairing freediving and Posidonia-meadow snorkelling at the Réserve du Larvotto with a sea-kayak coastal route to Cap Martin and Menton.
hook: Monaco's whole coastline is barely four kilometres long, but it packs a marine reserve, a rocky point that shelters two very different beaches, and a paddling route east into France that most visitors never try. This week works the water on foot from Larvotto, then extends it by kayak past Cap d'Ail and Cap Martin to Menton, with freediving as the constant thread underneath.

snapshot.Total Distance / Terrain: Roughly 18 km of coastline covered by kayak over the week; rocky coves, Posidonia meadow, sheltered marine reserve
snapshot.Getting There: Fly to Nice Côte d'Azur, then the coastal bus (Ligne 100) or a 20-minute train to Monaco-Monte-Carlo; no car needed for the week
snapshot.Who It Suits: Confident swimmers wanting a structured freediving introduction plus a genuine paddling route, on a single fixed base

itinerary.title: Larvotto and orientation
itinerary.morning: Arrive and settle in Larvotto, Monaco's only sand beach district, largely artificial but backed by real rock reef offshore. Walk the full length of the public beach and the adjoining private beach clubs to get the lay of the bay.
itinerary.afternoon: Snorkel session directly off the public beach into the Réserve du Larvotto, a protected zone of rocky reef and Posidonia oceanica seagrass that Monaco has kept off-limits to anchoring and spearfishing. The meadow starts within a hundred metres of the sand.
itinerary.evening: Walk the Larvotto seafront path toward the Grimaldi Forum as the beach clubs wind down; the water stays swimmable well past sunset in midsummer.
itinerary.dayStats: 1.5 water hours · Calm, sheltered bay, negligible current · mask, snorkel, fins, 2 mm shorty.

itinerary.title: Freediving introduction
itinerary.morning: A half-day freediving course with an FFESSM or AIDA-certified instructor based on this coast, both are the recognised certification bodies for French and international freediving, and any legitimate local outfit will hold one or the other. The morning covers breath-hold theory, equalisation, and static practice in the reserve's shallow water.
itinerary.afternoon: Open-water dynamic and depth practice along the reserve's rocky drop-off, working toward a first comfortable descent on a line. Visibility here is typically 8-15 m depending on recent boat traffic and swell.
itinerary.evening: Rest the ears and sinuses; an easy dinner in Monaco's Condamine market area rather than another water session.
itinerary.dayStats: 3 water hours · Calm, 20-24°C surface · freediving wetsuit 3 mm, weight belt, low-volume mask.

itinerary.title: Sea kayak to Cap d'Ail and Plage Mala
itinerary.morning: Launch a sea kayak from Larvotto and follow the coast west past the Rocher, Monaco's old town headland, and Fontvieille's harbour wall toward Cap d'Ail.
itinerary.afternoon: Round the cape to Plage Mala, a pair of coves reachable only by boat, on foot down a steep path, or by kayak. The water here is some of the clearest on this stretch, with a shallow reef good for a snorkel stop before paddling back.
itinerary.evening: Return to Monaco by kayak or, if the wind has picked up, arrange a pickup and take the coastal bus back with the boat on a roof rack.
itinerary.dayStats: 3.5 water hours · Light chop, 8-12 knots · sea kayak, spray skirt, buoyancy aid, reef shoes for the Mala landing.

itinerary.title: Cap Martin and the Sentier du Littoral
itinerary.morning: Kayak east this time, past Monaco's Port Hercule breakwater and along the base of Roquebrune-Cap-Martin toward Cap Martin itself.
itinerary.afternoon: Land at Cabbé and walk a section of the Promenade Le Corbusier, the coastal footpath along Cap Martin named for the architect, whose cabanon sits just above the water here and who drowned swimming off this coast in 1965. Snorkel the small bays either side of the point before paddling on.
itinerary.evening: Either continue by kayak toward Menton or turn back to Monaco depending on the afternoon wind; this is the week's longest open crossing and worth a conservative call.
itinerary.dayStats: 4 water hours · Moderate, 10-15 knots, light swell · sea kayak, wetsuit top, snorkel gear carried in a dry bag.

itinerary.title: Menton by water
itinerary.morning: Finish the coastal route into Menton's Vieux Port, passing beneath the old town's pastel façades from the water, a view almost nobody arriving by road ever sees.
itinerary.afternoon: Snorkel off Plage des Sablettes, Menton's town beach beside the harbour, then return the kayak by a support vehicle rather than paddling back against a building afternoon breeze.
itinerary.evening: Menton's old town for dinner, with the option of the train back to Monaco in twelve minutes.
itinerary.dayStats: 3 water hours · Building afternoon breeze, 12-18 knots by late afternoon · sea kayak, full wetsuit for the exposed final stretch.

itinerary.title: Deeper freediving and reserve return
itinerary.morning: A second freediving session back in the Réserve du Larvotto, now working toward greater depth and longer static holds with the skills from Day 2 consolidated. Buddy diving only, freediving alone in open water is the single most avoidable risk of the week.
itinerary.afternoon: Free afternoon. The Oceanographic Museum of Monaco, founded in 1910 on the Rocher, is worth the visit for anyone who has spent the week looking at this coast's marine life from below.
itinerary.evening: Easy dinner near Port Hercule, watching the superyachts come and go.
itinerary.dayStats: 2.5 water hours · Calm, 23-26°C surface in high summer · full freediving kit.

itinerary.title: Final snorkel and departure
itinerary.morning: A last unhurried snorkel session in the reserve, low intensity, purely to look rather than to train.
itinerary.afternoon: Return equipment, pack, and take the coastal bus or train to Nice for the flight home.
itinerary.dayStats: 1.5 water hours · Calm · mask, snorkel, fins.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel in the Larvotto district
accommodationStrategy.description: Staying within walking distance of the reserve removes the need for a car entirely and puts the beach, the dive shops and the kayak put-in within a ten-minute walk of the room. Ask for a room with balcony drying space for wetsuits.
accommodationStrategy.booking: three to four months ahead; Monaco has no low season.

accommodationStrategy.name: Serviced apartment, Fontvieille
accommodationStrategy.description: A short walk from Port de Fontvieille, useful as a quieter and often better-value alternative to Monte-Carlo proper, with easy access to the western kayak launch toward Cap d'Ail.

accommodationStrategy.name: Beaulieu-sur-Mer or Cap d'Ail base, day-tripping in
accommodationStrategy.description: Basing just across the border in France and taking the coastal train or bus into Monaco each day cuts accommodation cost substantially without losing access to the reserve or the kayak route.

logistics.emergency: Emergency number 112, and the French maritime emergency line 196, both reach CROSS Med, the regional maritime rescue coordination centre covering this coast; monitor VHF Channel 16 while kayaking.

other.text: Emergency number 112, and the French maritime emergency line 196, both reach CROSS Med, the regional maritime rescue coordination centre covering this coast; monitor VHF Channel 16 while kayaking.
Monaco's Division de Police Maritime et Aéroportuaire patrols the reserve and enforces its no-anchoring, no-spearfishing rules strictly.
Tidal range here is small, typically 20-40 cm, so kayak launch timing is not tide-dependent, unlike much of the Atlantic coast.

Water temperature: roughly 13-14°C in March, 19-20°C in June, 23-26°C July-September, cooling to 16-17°C by November. A 2 mm shorty suffices in high summer; add a 3 mm full suit for June or October freediving.

The mistral rarely hits Monaco directly but funnels gusts down the coastal valleys; the more relevant local pattern is the daily thermal sea breeze, building by early-to-mid afternoon from the south-east and dying at sunset, and the occasional libeccio bringing swell from the south-west.
Beach club sections of Larvotto operate under private concession in summer with sunbed fees; the public section at the eastern end remains free and gives full reserve access.
Freedive only with a buddy and never solo, regardless of experience level; the reserve's depth is enough to matter.

proTips: Paddle the Cap Martin and Menton legs in the morning, before the thermal breeze builds; afternoons past 14:00 regularly add a headwind on the return.
Book the freediving course for Day 2, not Day 1, a day of orientation swimming first improves equalisation on the actual course.
Land at Plage Mala on a weekday; the cove is small and a summer weekend fills the water with day-boats from Nice and Cannes.
Carry the kayak's dry bag with a phone in a waterproof case; there is no reliable phone signal dead zone here, but salt spray kills unprotected electronics fast.
Ask the kayak outfitter about a one-way rental with vehicle pickup at Menton; it turns the longest paddling day into a one-direction effort instead of an out-and-back.
Visit the Oceanographic Museum on the rest afternoon of Day 6 rather than at the start of the week, the fish are more interesting once you have spent days looking at them in the reserve.

packingNotes: A 2 mm shorty for summer snorkelling and a 3 mm full suit for freediving sessions and shoulder-season water.
Reef shoes for the rocky entries at Mala and Cap Martin; sand shoes alone are not enough.
A low-volume freediving mask, separate from a standard snorkelling mask if bringing personal gear.
A dry bag rated for kayak use, not just a beach dry bag, for the longer paddling days.
Reef-safe sunscreen; Monaco's beaches and the reserve are sensitive to standard sunscreen chemicals.
A light change of clothes carried in the kayak for the Menton lunch stop.
whatCouldGoWrong: **A strong afternoon breeze on the Menton leg.** Paddle early and arrange a vehicle return rather than fighting a building headwind on tired arms.
**Equalisation trouble on the freediving course.** This is common on Day 2; a good instructor will hold depth back rather than push it, and Day 6 gives a second, better attempt.
**Reduced visibility after a blow.** A few days of wind stir sediment near the shore; if the reserve looks murky, shift the snorkel to the rockier Cap d'Ail side, which clears faster.
**A fully booked beach club section.** The free public stretch of Larvotto always has reserve access regardless, so a sold-out sunbed day is a non-issue for the actual water time.
**Kayak rental gaps on peak weekends.** Reserve the Cap Martin and Menton days at least three days ahead in July and August; single-day walk-up rental is unreliable then.
